https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3v0.text: Figure caption, Watch: Buildings partially collapse in Indonesia after 7.7 earthquake By Emma Rossiter Published 3 hours ago Rescue teams in Indonesia have been searching for survivors of Saturday's major earthquake which left at least 47 people dead. The magnitude 7.7 quake struck the island of Flores shortly before 05:00 (22:00 GMT on Friday) and had a depth of 15km, Indonesia's meteorology and geophysics agency stated. Preliminary reports indicate hundreds of buildings have been severely damaged by the quake and the dozens of aftershocks that followed. However, the full scale of the disaster is still unclear, and news of a second earthquake of magnitude 6.9 at the other end of Indonesia served as a reminder of why they call this region the ring of fire. Tremors from Saturday's powerful earthquake were reportedly felt by residents as far west as Bima Regency and City, the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) agency said, but the Manggarai province is among the most affected. Preliminary data shows that 24 fatalities had been recorded there, meanwhile 17 deaths were recorded in East Manggarai province, three in Sikka province, and at least one in each of the Ngada, Ende and West Manggarai provinces. At least two others had been seriously injured and 11 slightly injured. The BNPB said aid was being sent to the affected areas with 10,500 packages arriving at the base operations so far. It will take time to assess the full extent of the destruction in the region, which is remote and mountainous. Image source, Reuters Image caption, The area is mountainous and the assessment will take time, officials say However, early reports indicate more than 150 houses had been severely damaged, as well as dozens of educational institutions, a number of healthcare facilities, places of worship, offices, and several other public facilities. Video taken at the port in Maumere - the largest town in Flores - showed large chunks of concrete breaking off the terminal building onto passengers waiting to board an inter-island ferry. Some were thrown into the sea when the gangway to a ship collapsed. Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, governor of East Nusa Tenggara province, told a news conference that they were killed in their sleep by collapsing rubble. Others, like Arnold Welianto, who lives in Talibura, a village near the coastline in Sikka, East Nusa Tenggara, were shaken out of their beds. "I was startled awake and immediately went to my child's room." He said. He also told the BBC that many people had already fled into the hills because the sea had also receded. Image caption, The earthquake struck around 600 miles (1,000km) away from Bali Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Rescue teams worked tirelessly through the day to free those trapped under the rubble While a tsunami warning was initially issued - leading some 2,000 people to self-evacuate - it was lifted around three hours after the initial jolt, when no significant sea level rise was detected. Landslides, however, did block access to some villages but the experienced rescue teams worked tirelessly through the day to free those trapped under the rubble. In Ruteng, a temporary medical tent was also assembled outside of a hospital to treat earthquake victims. Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, People could be seen moving inland after authorities issued a tsunami warning, which was later lifted The ongoing advice from BNPB is for people to remain calm and to stay away from coastal areas and structures showing signs of damage. Indonesia is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity, lying along the meeting point of three major tectonic plates. Photograph: MJ Photography/Alamy View image in fullscreen A statue in Georgetown, Guyana commemorating an 1823 uprising in Demerara, staged by enslaved abolitionists, which was a pivotal event in the fight to abolish slavery. Photograph: MJ Photography/Alamy Cotton Capital: ongoing series Slavery British corporation continued trafficking of enslaved Africans to Guyana 40 years after abolition Letter written in 1847 to Sandbach, Tinne and Company’s Liverpool office reveals it engaged in practice after receiving taxpayer-funded compensation, book says Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent Sun 23 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 23 Aug 2026 01.01 EDT Share When Britain abolished slavery, plantation owners from powerful families notoriously received huge sums in compensation, while those who were enslaved got nothing. Now evidence has come to light that Sandbach, Tinne and Company – a corporation closely linked to the merchants who got the biggest taxpayer-funded compensation payouts – continued to traffic enslaved Africans illegally after abolition to Guyana, in South America. The discovery is detailed in a book, Searching for My Slave Roots , by author Malik Al Nasir , who has been researching his family history. Its findings have inspired a new research project, Overwriting-Underwriting , which aims to uncover the financial networks behind enslavement and launches this month. The Slave Trade Act of 1807 abolished the trade in human beings in British territories. Then, in 1833, the Slavery Abolition Act banned slavery itself in most of the British empire. But an 1847 letter, written to Sandbach Tinne’s Liverpool office by Peter Miller Watson, who managed the company’s interests in Demerara, Guyana, refers to a ship from the company’s own fleet arriving with a “cargo of negroes”, including dozens of young children. View image in fullscreen Malik Al-Nasir whose book, Searching for My Slave Roots, has prompted research to uncover the financial networks behind enslavement. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian The letter details how the ship, called “the Parker”, was carrying “115 adult males, 86 adult females, 82 under 14 years, and 41 under 4 years,” adding: “There have been only three casualties during the passage – 1 man and 2 children – which Captain R. says may be attributed to the wretched state in which they had lived ashore.” Malik said: “Slavery had been abolished, so how do we know the people on the Parker weren’t indentured, or Africans liberated by the Royal Navy? Firstly, Watson specifically refers to them as cargo, and not passengers, when liberated Africans were not regarded as cargo, enslaved people were called cargo. “In referring to the ‘wretched state’ in which they had lived ashore, he’s saying they were shipped from land and are the architects of their own condition – if they had been previously enslaved blame would have been on their former masters, and they would not have been bought if they were sick. When [Watson] talks about casualties, he’s attributing the deaths as a loss of property. By process of deduction, we can see these are people illegally trafficked from Africa.” View image in fullscreen Charles Stuart Parker Jr was one of Sandbach Tinne’s principal shareholders in 1847. Photograph: Sandbach Tinne Collection of Cambridge Peter Miller Watson was a distant cousin of the British prime minister William Gladstone and the father of Andrew Watson, who became the first Black international footballer when he captained Scotland in the 1880s. Meanwhile, Sandbach Tinne, which was wound up in 1975, was the family business of the Sandbach and Tinne families, who, along with their collaborators and relatives in the Gladstone family, dominated the Demerara sugar trade. By the time of the 1847 letter, Sandbach Tinne and their subsidiaries had already received compensation equivalent to millions of pounds today for the “loss” of the people they enslaved before abolition. While family patriarch Samuel Sandbach had left the partnership in 1833, his son William Robertson Sandbach and son-in-law Charles Stuart Parker Jr were principal shareholders in 1847. British taxpayers’ debt for compensation payments to enslavers was only paid off in 2015 . “John Gladstone, the father of William Gladstone who owned plantations in Guyana and Jamaica, got the biggest single individual payout, while Sandbach Tinne got the second largest on aggregate – both were among architects of the compensation scheme,” Malik added. An 1823 uprising in Demerara , staged by enslaved abolitionists, was a pivotal event in the fight to abolish slavery, and began on a plantation owned by John Gladstone. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Monthly Sign up to Cotton Capital Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world after newsletter promotion But Al Nasir said an 1847 missionary account detailed how unregulated trading in enslaved people existed “south of the line” – meaning enslavers evading the Royal Navy’s blockade continued to traffic people from countries below the equator, such as Angola. View image in fullscreen William Robertson Sandbach received compensation equivalent to millions of pounds after abolition. Photograph: Sandbach Tinne Collection of Cambridge The Royal Navy’s West Africa Squadron – was tasked with intercepting slavers’ ships from 1808, with 1,600 sailors losing their lives. However, it is estimated that fewer than 10% of ships involved in enslaving people were intercepted. Even when ships were successfully stopped, “liberated Africans” faced military conscription and hard, unpaid labour under the apprenticeship and indentured labour systems. Overwriting – Underwriting launches at the Museum of Liverpool on Sunday, Unesco’s International Day of Remembrance of the Slave Trade and its Abolition. The launch event features renowned Jamaican academic Prof Verene Shepherd as keynote speaker, and a panel including Al Nasir and Lucy Moynihan from the University of Liverpool, chaired by Michelle Charters, the head of the International Slavery Museum. The initiative is inspired by research from Moynihan into John Gladstone’s insurance “risk books” as well as Al Nasir’s research into Sandbach Tinne. It is a pilot for the Connector project, a National Museums Liverpool initiative to develop understanding of transatlantic slavery’s legacies, supported by a £1m grant from Lloyd’s Register Foundation. Maritime group Lloyd’s Register apologised for its historical role in transatlantic slavery last year. Descendants of the Sandbach family and Gladstone family have both apologised for their ancestors’ involvement in slavery. https://www.politico.eu/article/berlin-e.text: BERLIN — Berlin’s leftist parties have a radical answer to the capital’s worsening housing crunch: seize the properties of the real estate giants they blame for ruining the city. That plan has become the most hotly contested issue in an election that takes place Sunday, with a coalition of left-wing parties poised to oust the conservative mayor of Germany’s capital and potentially usher in the first far-left mayor since the fall of the Berlin Wall. “The housing issue is the central social issue facing our city, and I have always said that, if I become mayor, I will pull out all the stops to make Berlin affordable again and lower rents,” said Elif Eralp, the lead candidate for the Left party. Advertisement Advertisement Eralp’s far-left party maintains a narrow lead in polls heading into the vote Sunday in Berlin, just ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which currently holds the mayor’s office. If her Left party is able to eke out a win, it’s likely to lead a coalition of left-wing parties that excludes the conservatives, who have fought such plans. The Left party, which traces part of its history to East Germany’s communist party, is enjoying a political revival after winning a new wave of support from young voters mobilized by the far right’s rise. For its Berlin campaign, the party has taken inspiration from New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, employing his focus on cost-of-living issues as a model . Once a city known for cheap rents that helped cultivate an international, bohemian culture, affordable housing has become a particularly pressing issue in the German capital in recent years. Fewer than one in six residents of the city own the home they live in, while rents have risen by about 70% over the past decade. The Left party is running on a plan to expropriate properties from real estate companies that own more than 3,000 apartments. It’s an idea that has widespread support in a city that has historically leaned left. Nearly 60 percent of voters backed expropriating properties from major real estate companies in a 2021 referendum. The organization that initiated that referendum estimates that the city could forcibly buy as many as 220,000 apartments for up to 60 percent of their market value — amounting to a total of €18 billion. That money, they argue, could be recovered by the city over the course of a century from rental income. Stefan Evers, the CDU’s lead candidate in Berlin, says fear of a Left party win is already causing harm to the city’s real estate market. Advertisement Advertisement “Many housing companies are steering well clear of Berlin simply because this debate is already taking place today, because there is a political party that may come to power and actually wants to implement this,” he told RTL television. “It will prevent new apartments from being built — apartments that are already in short supply today. And it will drive up rents. And that is exactly the opposite of what we want.” Leftist ‘paradigm shift’ The Greens in Berlin, polling in fourth place with around 15 percent support, are the only other party to fully support the expropriation plans, and have expressed their ambition to push it through in coalition with the Left party. “The question is whether, after this election, the right policies will finally be put in place and we can usher in a paradigm shift,” said Katrin Schmidberger, a Green lawmaker sitting in Berlin’s state parliament. That leaves the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), polling fifth with 12 percent support, as a potential moderating force. The Left party would need both the Greens and SPD to have enough seats to form a government in Berlin. But the SPD’s lead candidate, Steffen Krach, opposes expropriation, favoring other measures to lower rents. Krach may have somewhat limited scope to hinder the plans following a corruption probe involving accusations he accepted illicit campaign donations while he held an earlier office in Hanover. Krach, who denies any wrongdoing, has lost political capital as a result of the accusations. Right-wing parties have meanwhile railed against the expropriation plans in Berlin, including the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is polling at an unexpectedly strong 18% — putting it in third place, just a few percentage points behind the Left party. Advertisement Advertisement “With the Left party, above all, what you get is new socialism,” Kristin Brinker, the AfD’s lead candidate in Berlin, told Welt TV. “We know — if we look back — that Berlin has already experienced socialism, and given the state of the real estate market at that time, that’s something many people don’t want.” Legal hurdles The AfD has no chance of taking real political power in Berlin, as all other parties have ruled out working with the far right. But a potential left-wing coalition would still need to overcome many hurdles. Although an expert commission concluded in 2023 that the expropriation proposal is legally feasible, implementing it would be tricky. Such a move be founded on Article 15 of Germany’s constitution, which allows “land, natural resources, and means of production” to be transferred to “common ownership.” But that provision has never been applied. If implemented, the expropriation policy would almost certainly be challenged before the constitutional court, with experts arguing the judges could rule either way. Merz’s government has vowed to prevent the expropriation of real estate companies at the state level by adopting a national law against the practice. But that text hasn’t been drafted and experts are, once again, divided on whether the federal government would have the legal ability to block local efforts. Despite the obstacles, the Left party, believes it will prevail. “As for the federal government’s proposal, I’ll say this very clearly: we don’t want any interference … And as a lawyer, I’ll also say clearly that I have very serious doubts about whether that is constitutional,” the party’s lead candidate Eralp told reporters in Berlin earlier this month. “That’s why we stand by our position: We want to expropriate.” Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Huntington Beach fire department via Facebook View image in fullscreen A sign warns of a shark sighting in Huntington Beach, California, on 13 October 2026. Photograph: Huntington Beach fire department via Facebook California Southern California beach closes after sighting of great white shark ‘exhibiting aggressive behavior’ Two-mile stretch of Huntington Beach closed after sighting at location popular with surfers and swimmers Dani Anguiano Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.40 EDT Last modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A popular southern California beach was closed after a great white shark was reportedly spotted “exhibiting aggressive behavior” on Tuesday afternoon. The Huntington Beach fire department said there was a “credible report” of a 10-12ft great white shark circling near a lifeguard tower, which is considered aggressive behavior according to the city’s marine safety division’s “shark response protocols”. Officials closed a two-mile long stretch of beach near the tower between Seapoint and the Huntington Beach pier through Wednesday afternoon, and said workers had posted warning signs and notified visitors. “Please follow all posted signs and instructions from lifeguards. Public safety remains our top priority,” the city’s fire department said in a statement. The Orange county beach is popular with surfers and swimmers. California saw an unusually high number of great white sharks over the summer as juveniles fled warm waters in Mexico amid El Niño. Experts said humans shouldn’t be alarmed. Shark incidents involving bites are “extremely rare” in California , according to the state’s department of fish and wildlife. There have been fewer than 250 shark incidents in the state since 1950, and fewer than 20 were fatal. Scientists agree that such incidents are generally “exploratory bites” as a result of sharks investigating “unusual objects in their environment, such as kayaks”, the fish and wildlife department said.
